# Summary of European Commission Decision DMA.100193 – Alphabet – Google Search – Article 6(5) DMA

---

## 0. Identification

The **European Commission** adopted **Decision DMA.100193** on **23 July 2026** under **Articles 29(1)(a), 30(1)(a) and 31(1)(h) of Regulation (EU) 2022/1925 (Digital Markets Act, "DMA")** against **Alphabet Inc.** (including all entities it controls, collectively **"Alphabet"**) for non-compliance with **Article 6(5) DMA** regarding its **online search engine (OSE) core platform service Google Search**.
This is a **non-compliance decision** imposing a **fine**, a **cease-and-desist order** and **periodic penalty payments**. The text is a **non-confidential version** with redactions.
An **appeal is possible to the General Court of the European Union** under Article 263 TFEU; the decision does not mention any appeal lodged to date.
**One-sentence summary**: The Commission finds that **Alphabet has not complied with Article 6(5) DMA from 7 March 2024** by treating its own distinct or additional services (e.g. comparison-shopping, flights, trains, lodging, local places, Google Maps, translation, sports results, games) **more favourably in ranking on Google Search than similar third-party services**, and imposes a **fine of EUR 460 000 000**, a **cease-and-desist order within 60 days** and **periodic penalty payments** in case of continued non-compliance.

---

---

## 1. Facts

### Who

**Alphabet Inc.** is a **publicly traded company** headquartered in **Mountain View, California, USA**, operating globally in internet-related services and products, including **Google Search** ([recital 1](cite:1)).
**Google Ireland Ltd**, an Alphabet subsidiary established in Ireland, is the **legal entity providing Google Search in the Union** ([recital 1](cite:2)).
Alphabet was **designated as a gatekeeper** for **Google Search** (among other core platform services) by Commission decision of **5 September 2023** ([recital 4](cite:3)).
Alphabet’s **total worldwide turnover** in the business year ending **31 December 2025 was USD 402 836 000 000** (approximately **EUR 356 509 860 000**) ([recital 675](cite:4)).

The **businesses and users disadvantaged** are **third-party services similar to Alphabet’s distinct or additional services** ranked on Google Search, including:
- **Vertical search services (VSSs)** such as **comparison-shopping services (CSSs)** (e.g. Idealo, Kelkoo, Guenstiger) ([recital 198](cite:5)).
- **Flights, trains, lodging and local places intermediation services** (e.g. Skyscanner, Kayak, Expedia, Booking.com, TripAdvisor) ([recital 293](cite:6)).
- **Online map services** (e.g. Apple Maps, Bing Maps) ([recital 501](cite:7)).
- **Translation, sports information and games services** (e.g. DeepL, Linguee, Kicker.de, solitaired.com) ([recital 529](cite:8)).

The decision **does not state the number of disadvantaged parties**.

### What

The **practice found** is that **Alphabet treats more favourably in ranking on Google Search its own distinct or additional services** than **similar services of third parties** ([recital 2](cite:9)).
The **gatekeeper’s own services favoured** include:
- **Intermediation services** for **products** (Google Shopping), **flights**, **trains**, **lodging** and **local places** (e.g. restaurants) ([recital 113](cite:10)).
- **Google Maps** ([recital 493](cite:11)).
- **Content-related services**: **translation** (Google Translate), **sports information** and **games** ([recital 523](cite:12)).

The **third-party services disadvantaged** are **similar services** in the same categories (e.g. CSSs, VSSs for flights/trains/lodging/places, map services, translation services, sports information services, games websites) ([recital 198](cite:13)).

**Effects on business users, competitors and end users** as described by the Commission:
- **Third-party services are ranked less prominently** on the **Google Search Engine Results Page (SERP)**, reducing their **visibility and traffic** ([recital 213](cite:14)).
- **Alphabet’s own services are embedded in dedicated units** (e.g. product ads unit, products unit, airlines unit, trains unit, lodging unit, places unit, translation unit, sports unit, games unit) **at the top of the SERP**, with **enhanced features** (e.g. interactive maps, query shortcut chips, preview pages) that **facilitate comparison and transactions directly on the SERP** ([recital 93](cite:15)).
- **Third-party services cannot match this prominence** as they are **relegated to organic results, rich web results or dedicated tabs** (e.g. ‘Product comparison sites’, ‘Flight sites’, ‘Places sites’) that **do not offer the same level of interactivity or visibility** ([recital 214](cite:16)).

**Measures the gatekeeper proposed or tested**:
- **March 2024 changes**: Alphabet introduced **new designs for third-party services** (e.g. rich web results for CSSs, dedicated CSS units, new tabs for VSSs) to **increase their prominence** ([recital 226](cite:17)).
- The Commission **found these measures insufficient** to ensure **equal prominence** between Alphabet’s own services and similar third-party services ([recital 248](cite:18)).

**Uncertainties or open points the Commission leaves**:
- The Commission **does not prescribe specific compliance measures** but requires Alphabet to **ensure equal treatment** in ranking between its own services and similar third-party services ([recital 713](cite:19)).

### Where

The **territory concerned** is the **European Union** ([recital 670](cite:20))).

### When

- **Start of the obligation**: **7 March 2024** (six months after Alphabet’s designation as gatekeeper for Google Search) ([recital 5](cite:21)%20of%20Regulation)).
- **Non-compliance is ongoing** at the date of the decision (**23 July 2026**) ([recital 641](cite:22)).
- **Opening of proceedings**: **25 March 2024** ([recital 7](cite:23)).
- **Preliminary findings**: **19 March 2025** ([recital 10](cite:24)).
- **Alphabet’s replies**: **18 May 2025** (response to preliminary findings) ([recital 15](cite:25)).
- **Date of the decision**: **23 July 2026** ([header](cite:26)).

---

---

## 2. Procedure

- **Origin**: The Commission **designated Alphabet as a gatekeeper** for Google Search on **5 September 2023** ([recital 4](cite:27)).
- **Steps**:
  - **Compliance reports**: Alphabet submitted **annual compliance reports** on **7 March 2024**, **6 March 2025** and **6 March 2026**, confirming no changes to its March 2024 measures ([recital 6](cite:28)).
  - **Opening of proceedings**: **25 March 2024** ([recital 7](cite:29)).
  - **Requests for information (RFIs)**: Four RFIs sent to Alphabet between **6 May 2024 and 2 August 2024** ([recital 8](cite:30)).
  - **Preliminary findings**: **19 March 2025** ([recital 10](cite:31)).
  - **Access to file**: Granted to Alphabet’s external advisers between **24 March 2025 and 8 April 2025** ([recital 14](cite:32))).
  - **Alphabet’s reply**: **18 May 2025** ([recital 15](cite:33)).
- **Rights of defence**:
  - Alphabet **requested access to the file** on **20 March 2025** and **raised concerns** about redactions ([recitals 11-12](cite:34)).
  - The Commission **rejected some claims** but granted access to **non-confidential versions of cited documents** and **full file access to external advisers** ([recitals 13-14](cite:35)).
- **Procedural objections raised by Alphabet**:
  - **Scope of investigation**: Alphabet argued the Commission **exceeded the scope of the Opening Decision** by including **content-related queries** (e.g. sports, translation, games) and **free units** (e.g. products unit) ([recital 604](cite:36)).
  - **Breach of sound administration**: Alphabet claimed the Commission **adopted a prejudicial position**, **did not conduct a genuine investigation**, **disregarded third-party evidence** and **relied on complainants’ arguments** ([recital 616](cite:37)).
  - **Access to file**: Alphabet argued it was **denied full access to the file** ([recital 631](cite:38)).
- **Outcome of procedural objections**:
  - The Commission **rejected all objections**, finding the investigation **within scope**, **impartial** and **respectful of Alphabet’s rights of defence** ([recital 607](cite:39)).
- **Parallel proceedings**: The decision **does not mention any parallel proceedings** before national authorities or courts.
- **Precedents or case law cited**:
  - **Google Shopping** (General Court and Court of Justice judgments) ([recital 81](cite:40)).
  - **ByteDance v Commission** (General Court judgment on DMA procedural framework) ([recital 634](cite:41)).

---

---

## 3. Legal basis

- **Obligation breached**: **Article 6(5) DMA**, which prohibits gatekeepers from **treating more favourably in ranking and related indexing and crawling their own services or products than similar services or products of third parties** ([recital 18](cite:42)%20of%20Regulation)).
- **Legal framework**:
  - **Recital 51 DMA**: Clarifies that gatekeepers may **reserve better ranking for their own services**, including **other core platform services embedded in OSE results** ([recital 20](cite:43)).
  - **Recital 52 DMA**: Defines **more favourable treatment** as **any differentiated or preferential treatment in ranking**, including **all forms of relative prominence** (display, rating, linking, voice results) ([recital 21](cite:44)).
  - **Article 2(23) DMA**: Defines **search results** broadly as **any information returned in response to a query**, including **paid or unpaid results, direct answers or embedded services** ([recital 23](cite:45))).
  - **Article 2(22) DMA**: Defines **ranking** as **relative prominence or relevance given to search results** ([recital 24](cite:46))).
- **Points examined and not retained**:
  - The Commission **did not retain Alphabet’s argument** that **OSEs and OISs overlap** in purpose, finding a **clear legal distinction** between the two ([recital 54](cite:47)).
  - The Commission **did not retain Alphabet’s argument** that **user perceptions or expectations** should determine whether a service is distinct or additional to an OSE, as this would **undermine consistent interpretation** of Article 6(5) DMA ([recital 61](cite:48)).

---

---
---
## 4. Arguments

### Alphabet’s arguments on the existence of distinct or additional services
**Alphabet argues that** the units on Google Search (e.g. product ads unit, products unit, airlines unit) **are not distinct or additional services** but **part of the OSE’s purpose** to provide **relevant results** to users.
- Alphabet claims that **OSEs may display results in any format** (including direct answers, grouped results, transaction-related information) and **from any data source** (crawling, data feeds, licensed data) ([recital 50](cite:49)).
- Alphabet argues that **OSEs facilitate transactions** and **enable users to compare results**, which is **consistent with their purpose** ([recital 42](cite:50)).
- Alphabet contends that **query shortcut chips** are **input mechanisms for users** and **not indicative of distinct services** ([recital 151](cite:51)).
- Alphabet argues that **the units do not have full OIS functionality** and **cannot operate as separate services** ([recital 150](cite:52)).

**The Commission answers that**:
- A service is **distinct or additional to an OSE** if it **has a different purpose** (e.g. **transactional intermediation**) or **is not assembled by searching in principle all websites** ([recital 28](cite:53)).
- **Functionalities** (e.g. filtering, comparing offers, query shortcut chips) and **data sources** (e.g. data feeds from pre-selected websites) **indicate a distinct service** when they **go beyond the purpose of an OSE** ([recital 158](cite:54)).
- **User expectations or perceptions are irrelevant** for determining the purpose of a service ([recital 61](cite:55)).

**Outcome**: **Rejected**.

---

### Alphabet’s arguments on the similarity of third-party services
**Alphabet argues that** the Commission **failed to establish an objective benchmark** for determining **similar third-party services** and that **similarity should be equated with substitutability** under competition law.
- Alphabet claims that **third-party services are not similar** if they **do not serve the same purpose for users** or **are not alternatives** ([recital 69](cite:56)).

**The Commission answers that**:
- **Similarity** is determined by **comparing functionalities and tasks performed** by the services, **not by substitutability** ([recital 65](cite:57)).
- **Differences in monetisation or business models** are **not material** for the assessment ([recital 207](cite:58)).

**Outcome**: **Rejected**.

---
### Alphabet’s arguments on more favourable treatment
**Alphabet argues that** the Commission **misapplied the legal test** for **more favourable treatment** under Article 6(5) DMA.
- Alphabet claims that **Article 6(5) DMA is about equality of opportunity, not outcome**, and that **differential treatment is not prohibited if it is not arbitrary or discriminatory** ([recital 79](cite:59))).
- Alphabet argues that **the Commission failed to show a tangible advantage** for Alphabet’s services or a **commensurate disadvantage** for third parties ([recital 80](cite:60)).
- Alphabet contends that **the March 2024 changes** (e.g. rich web results for CSSs, dedicated tabs for VSSs) **compensated for any favourable treatment** ([recital 225](cite:61)).

**The Commission answers that**:
- **More favourable treatment** includes **any differentiated or preferential treatment in ranking**, regardless of **tangible effects** ([recital 75](cite:62)).
- The **March 2024 changes did not ensure equal prominence** between Alphabet’s services and similar third-party services ([recital 248](cite:63)).
- **Conditioning equal prominence on requirements that do not apply to Alphabet’s own services** (e.g. requiring third-party CSSs to become business partners) **does not eliminate favourable treatment** ([recital 78](cite:64)).

**Outcome**: **Rejected**.

---
### Alphabet’s arguments on the fine
**Alphabet argues that** a fine is **not warranted** because:
- The case is **novel** (first application of Article 6(5) DMA) and the Commission **refrains from imposing fines in novel cases** under competition law ([recital 654](cite:65)).
- **Article 6(5) DMA lacks clarity and specificity** ([recital 656](cite:66))).
- **Compliance is complex** and requires **balancing stakeholder interests** ([recital 657](cite:67)).
- Alphabet **acted in good faith** and **engaged constructively** with the Commission ([recital 658](cite:68)).

**The Commission answers that**:
- **Negligence is established** as Alphabet **could not have been unaware** of the non-compliance, given the **clear language of Article 6(5) DMA**, **Commission guidance** and **repeated exchanges** with Alphabet ([recital 647](cite:69)).
- **Novelty does not preclude fines** under the DMA, which **expressly provides for fines** for non-compliance with Article 6 ([recital 659](cite:70)).
- **Good faith engagement does not offset non-compliance** ([recital 666](cite:71)).

**Outcome**: **Rejected**.

---
### Alphabet’s arguments on periodic penalty payments
**Alphabet argues that** periodic penalty payments are **unwarranted** because:
- The Commission **did not provide reasoning** for imposing the **maximum amount** ([recital 718](cite:72)).
- Imposing the **maximum amount would be contrary to Commission precedent** ([recital 719](cite:73)).
- The **maximum amount is only appropriate in the most egregious cases** ([recital 720](cite:74)).
- The Commission should **take into account mitigating factors** ([recital 721](cite:75)).

**The Commission answers that**:
- **Reasoning was provided** in the Preliminary Findings ([recital 722](cite:76)).
- **Precedents are not binding**, and the **circumstances of this case justify periodic penalty payments** ([recital 723](cite:77)).
- **Mitigating factors do not offset the seriousness of the non-compliance** ([recital 726](cite:78)).

**Outcome**: **Rejected**.

---
### Remaining weak points
The Commission **partly conceded** that:
- **User expectations or perceptions are subjective** and **not a reliable basis** for determining the purpose of a service ([recital 61](cite:79)).
- **The DMA is a new regulatory framework**, and this is **one of the first non-compliance decisions** under Article 6(5) DMA, which **justifies a mitigating factor** in the fine calculation ([recital 689](cite:80)).

The Commission **left open** whether:
- **Further changes by Alphabet** (beyond the March 2024 measures) **could achieve compliance** ([recital 713](cite:81)).

---
---
---
## 5. Decision

### Fine
- **Amount**: **EUR 460 000 000** ([operative part, Article 2](cite:82)).
- **Criteria used** (Article 30(4) DMA):
  - **Gravity**: **Serious**, as the non-compliance **covered the entire Union**, **affected a large number of users and businesses**, involved **multiple services** and Alphabet is a **very large company** ([recitals 669-676](cite:83)%202022/1925%20lists%20the%20gravity)).
  - **Duration**: **Medium** (approximately **28 months**, from **7 March 2024 to 23 July 2026**) ([recital 684](cite:84)).
  - **Recurrence**: **Not applicable** (first DMA non-compliance decision for Alphabet) ([recital 687](cite:85)).
  - **Mitigating circumstance**: **Novelty of the DMA framework** ([recital 689](cite:86)).
- **Cap**: The fine is **below the 10 % cap** of Alphabet’s **total worldwide turnover** (EUR 356 509 860 000) ([recital 701](cite:87))).

### Cease and desist
- **Content**: Alphabet must **bring the non-compliance effectively to an end** within **60 calendar days** from notification of the decision ([operative part, Article 3](cite:88)).
- **Obligations**:
  - **Cease treating its own distinct or additional services more favourably in ranking** than similar third-party services on Google Search ([recital 710](cite:89)).
  - **Ensure equal treatment** in terms of **relative prominence** between its own services and similar third-party services ([recital 711](cite:90)).
  - **Provide explanations** on how it plans to comply within **60 days** ([operative part, Article 3](cite:91)).
  - **Refrain from repeating the non-compliant conduct** or any conduct with the **same or equivalent object or effect** ([operative part, Article 3](cite:92)).

### Periodic penalty payments
- **Ceiling**: **Not exceeding the limit stipulated in Article 31(1) DMA** (up to **5 % of average daily worldwide turnover**) ([operative part, Article 4](cite:93)).
- **Starting point**: **From the date on which compliance is due** (after 60 days from notification) **until the date of compliance** ([operative part, Article 4](cite:94)).

---
---
## 6. Appeal

- **Court**: **General Court of the European Union** (Article 263 TFEU) ([recital 642](cite:95)).
- **Deadline**: **To be checked by the tool** (the decision does not specify the deadline) ([recital 642](cite:96)).
- **Appeal lodged**: The decision **does not mention any appeal** lodged to date.
